guides.title: Ritual — How Sacred Actions Work
guides.summary: Ritual is patterned, formalised action that societies treat as consequential, and this guide explains what it is, how it functions and why humans everywhere do it. It covers rites of passage, sacrifice, purity, performative words, the cognitive and signalling theories of ritual, ritual calendars, secular ritual, and how rituals fail.

sections.heading: What ritual is, and why it is everywhere
sections.body:
No human society has ever been found without ritual. Archaeologists digging Neanderthal sites at Shanidar in Iraq and Sima de los Huesos in Spain argue over whether deliberate burial and the deposit of bodies in a pit constitute ritual, but by the time anatomically modern humans appear in the record the evidence is unambiguous: ochre-stained burials with grave goods at Sungir in Russia around thirty-four thousand years ago, where a boy and a girl were interred with roughly ten thousand laboriously drilled mammoth-ivory beads, representing thousands of hours of labour buried in the ground. Whatever the people who did that believed, they were prepared to destroy enormous value to do something correctly.

Ritual is best defined not by its content but by its form. It is action that is formalised, repeated, prescribed rather than improvised, performed at set times or in response to set occasions, and understood by its performers to matter in a way that ordinary action does not. Lighting a candle to see is practical action. Lighting a candle in a particular place, at a particular moment, in a prescribed order, while saying prescribed words, is ritual — even when the candle produces exactly the same light.

The crucial and often missed point is that ritual is not defined by belief. A ritual can be performed by someone with vivid faith, by someone with none, by a child who understands nothing, and by an official doing a job, and it remains the same ritual. Many traditions care intensely about whether the act was done correctly and comparatively little about the interior state of the performer, a priority anthropologists call orthopraxy — right practice — as opposed to orthodoxy, right belief. Judaism, Confucian ritual practice, Vedic sacrifice and much of Roman religion are strongly orthopraxic; the Roman formula was that the rite must be repeated from the beginning if a single word was misspoken or a mouse squeaked at the wrong moment.

The scope of the word is wider than religion. Courtrooms have rituals, as do parliaments, armies, sports teams, universities at graduation and families at breakfast. A judge in a wig, a soldier saluting, a jury swearing an oath, a bride walking a particular route: these are formalised, prescribed, consequential acts that would strike an outside observer as no less strange than an offering to an ancestor. Treating religious and secular ritual as the same kind of thing is not a way of debunking religion; it is a way of noticing that formalised action is a general human technology, applied to whatever a community treats as too important to leave to improvisation.

Understanding ritual therefore means answering a mechanical question rather than a theological one: what does patterned, costly, prescribed action actually do, for individuals and for groups, that ordinary purposive action does not?

sections.heading: The problem ritual solves: talk is cheap, action is expensive
sections.body:
Start with a hard practical problem that every human group faces. Cooperation, especially among people who are not close kin, requires trust, and trust requires knowing who is genuinely committed. But commitment is invisible. Anyone can say they are loyal, devout, honest, or one of us. Words cost nothing, and precisely because they cost nothing they carry little information. Biologists call this the problem of cheap talk, and it has a well-understood solution: signals become credible when they are costly enough that a faker would not bother to send them.

This is the logic of costly signalling theory, developed from Amotz Zahavi's handicap principle in evolutionary biology and applied to human ritual by researchers including William Irons, Richard Sosis and Joseph Henrich. A signal is believable in proportion to what it costs the sender relative to the benefit of deceiving. A peacock's tail is honest because a sick bird cannot grow one. In human terms, a man who fasts for a month, undergoes painful scarification, gives away a tenth of his income, learns thousands of lines of liturgy, or refuses profitable work one day in seven has demonstrated something a mere declaration could never demonstrate.

The empirical support for this is unusually concrete. Sosis and Eric Bressler examined two hundred nineteen nineteenth-century American communes and found that religious communes survived on average four times longer than secular ones, and that among religious communes, longevity correlated strongly with the number of costly requirements imposed on members — dietary restrictions, dress codes, restrictions on outside contact. Among secular communes the same correlation was absent, suggesting the costliness works when embedded in a framework that makes the costs meaningful rather than merely arbitrary.

Ritual solves a second, related problem: coordination. Even people who all want the same thing must know that the others want it and know that the others know. Economists call this common knowledge, and it is genuinely different from everyone privately agreeing. A public ritual generates common knowledge cheaply and reliably, because everyone can see everyone else participating and can see that they can see. This is why oaths are sworn publicly, why coronations and inaugurations are staged rather than filed as paperwork, and why revolutionary movements hold mass rallies that convey no new information to any individual present.

There is a third function: ritual manages the situations where ordinary action fails. Death, birth, illness, harvest, war and weather all present outcomes that matter enormously and that people cannot fully control. Bronisław Malinowski, working in the Trobriand Islands in the 1910s, made the observation that has anchored the field ever since: Trobriand fishermen performed elaborate magical rites before venturing into the dangerous open ocean, and almost none before fishing in the safe inner lagoon. The variable was not ignorance. It was uncertainty and risk.

sections.heading: The grammar of ritual action: formality, invariance and redundancy
sections.body:
Rituals across wildly unrelated cultures share formal features so consistently that they amount to a grammar, and cataloguing them is the first analytical step in understanding any particular rite.

The first feature is formality: restricted, elevated or archaic language, stylised posture and gesture, special clothing, and constrained options for what may be said or done. Ritual language is frequently not everyday language — Latin in the Catholic Mass until the 1960s, Hebrew in synagogue, Sanskrit in Hindu rites, Classical Arabic in Muslim prayer, Church Slavonic in Orthodox liturgy, and archaic English in traditional Anglican worship. Maurice Bloch argued that this formalisation actually strips language of its ordinary argumentative power: you cannot debate a chanted formula the way you can debate a proposition, which is precisely why the formalised version carries authority.

The second is invariance and repetition. Rituals are done the same way each time, and being done the same way is part of what makes them work. Where an engineer improves a process by refining it, a ritual specialist preserves it, and deviation is not innovation but error. Roman augury, Vedic sacrifice, Japanese tea ceremony and Orthodox liturgy all include explicit provisions for what happens when the sequence is broken, and the answer is usually to begin again.

The third is redundancy: rituals say the same thing many times, in several channels at once. A wedding may assert the union through words, through the joining of hands, through an exchanged object, through a shared cup, through a change of dress, through a procession and through a signed document. This is not inefficiency. Redundancy is how a message survives noise, and how it reaches participants who process meaning differently — the child who understands nothing verbal still sees the hands joined.

The fourth is what Roy Rappaport called the encoding of messages the performer did not compose. In ritual, the participant transmits a message that was fixed before they arrived. By performing it, they accept it publicly, whatever they privately think. Rappaport argued this is the origin of the concept of obligation itself: participation is a self-referential public acceptance of an order, and thereafter deviation counts as violation rather than mere difference.

The fifth is marked separation from ordinary time and space. A ritual has a threshold — a door, a gate, a curtain, a removal of shoes, a washing of hands, a bell, an opening formula — and a closing that returns participants to ordinary life. Anthropologists call this framing, and it does real cognitive work: it tells participants that what follows is not to be interpreted by everyday rules, which is why the same words that would be a lie in conversation are not a lie in a rite, and why swallowing a wafer is not a snack.

sections.heading: Rites of passage and the three-phase structure
sections.body:
The single most productive idea in the study of ritual was published in 1909 by the Belgian-born French ethnographer Arnold van Gennep in Les rites de passage. Comparing initiation, marriage, birth, funeral and seasonal rites from across the ethnographic record, he noticed that they were not a miscellany but variations on one underlying architecture, and that the architecture had three phases.

The first is separation, in which the person is detached from their previous social position. Practically this means removing them from ordinary company and stripping the markers of the old status: hair is cut, ordinary clothing is exchanged for a shroud or plain garment, the name may be surrendered, and the initiate is taken from the village into the bush, the novice from the world into the cloister, the recruit from home to a camp where their possessions are confiscated. The old self is symbolically killed, and initiation rites very often use explicit death imagery for exactly this reason.

The second is the transition or margin, which van Gennep called liminal from the Latin limen, a threshold. Here the person is neither what they were nor what they will become. They are structurally invisible, frequently subject to prohibitions and ordeals, taught secret knowledge, and often treated as dangerous or polluting because they occupy no proper category. Liminal periods range from minutes to years: a bride between her father's house and her husband's, a corpse between death and burial, a monastic novitiate, boot camp, the years between matriculation and graduation.

The third is incorporation or aggregation, in which the person is reattached to society in the new status. New clothes, a new name, a new title, a communal meal, the first public act in the new role. Crucially, the community must witness this, because the change being wrought is social rather than private. A person cannot make themselves a spouse, a citizen, a doctor or an elder by deciding to be one.

Van Gennep's insight is that these phases are not equally weighted in every rite. Funerals emphasise separation; weddings emphasise incorporation; initiations emphasise the liminal middle. He also observed that the same territorial logic applies to physical passage — crossing a border, entering a house, passing through a gate — and that thresholds are ritually marked in a startling proportion of cultures.

The framework's power is diagnostic. Given any transition a society treats as significant, it predicts that a rite will exist, that it will have these phases, and that the middle phase will be marked by ambiguity and danger. Where a modern society has weakened or abolished a rite of passage — adolescence in much of the industrialised world is the standard example — the transition still happens, but without a public marker, without a defined endpoint, and without a community obliged to acknowledge that it is complete.

sections.heading: Liminality, communitas and the anti-structure of ritual
sections.body:
Van Gennep's middle phase was taken up and hugely extended by the Scottish anthropologist Victor Turner, whose fieldwork among the Ndembu of Zambia in the 1950s produced the most influential body of ritual theory of the twentieth century. Turner argued that the liminal phase is not merely a gap between statuses but a distinct social condition with its own properties, and that societies depend on it.

Liminal persons, he observed, are stripped of the marks that ordinarily distinguish people from one another. Initiates wear identical clothing or none, are given identical food, are shaved alike, are humbled, are subjected to the same treatment, and are forbidden to claim rank. Because the ordinary structure of hierarchy is suspended, what emerges among them is what Turner called communitas: an intense, unstructured, egalitarian bond between people who are experiencing the same thing at the same time. Anyone who has been through basic training, a long pilgrimage, a hospital ward, a disaster or a demanding retreat will recognise it — a feeling of unmediated fellowship that dissolves when normal roles resume.

Turner's key theoretical move was to see structure and communitas as a necessary pair rather than opposites. Ordinary social life runs on structure: differentiated roles, rank, property, obligations. Structure is efficient and it is also alienating, and it accumulates resentment. Rituals of liminality periodically dissolve structure, generate communitas, and then reinstate structure with the participants having been reminded that the hierarchy is a human arrangement rather than a fact of nature. Carnival, the medieval Feast of Fools, saturnalia in which masters served slaves, and rites in which a chief is publicly insulted before enthronement all fit this pattern; Turner called them rituals of status reversal, and argued they strengthen the order they mock.

He also distinguished liminal from what he called liminoid phenomena, which are the voluntary, individually chosen analogues found in complex industrial societies: theatre, festivals, sport, music scenes, travel, art. These offer some of the same suspension of ordinary structure but without obligation and without a guaranteed return to a changed status, which is why, in his account, they are experienced as recreation rather than transformation.

The concept has proven exportable and is now used well beyond anthropology, in studies of migration, unemployment, terminal illness, refugee camps, prison and organisational change. Its analytical value lies in a specific prediction: people in a prolonged liminal state, where the ending is indefinite and there is no rite to complete it, experience characteristic distress — a sense of being suspended, unable to plan, and unrecognised. The remedy this framework suggests is not therapy for an individual failing but the provision of a marked, witnessed ending: a definite date, a public acknowledgement, and a named new status to enter. This is why organisations that handle redundancy well stage a leaving occasion, and why armies that demobilise soldiers abruptly and privately produce worse outcomes than those that stage a formal return.

sections.heading: The sacred, the profane and collective effervescence
sections.body:
The foundational sociological account of ritual belongs to Émile Durkheim, whose Elementary Forms of Religious Life appeared in 1912. Working from ethnographic reports of Aboriginal Australian totemism, which he took to be the simplest available religion, Durkheim proposed that the fundamental religious distinction is not between gods and humans but between two categories of thing: the sacred, which is set apart, protected by prohibitions and treated as inviolable, and the profane, which is ordinary, usable and negotiable. What is sacred varies enormously between societies; that the distinction exists does not.

Ritual, in this account, is the machinery that creates and maintains the boundary. Durkheim's central mechanism is collective effervescence: when a dispersed group assembles and acts in unison — chanting, dancing, drumming, moving together — participants experience an emotional intensity that clearly does not originate in any individual. They feel acted upon by a power greater than themselves, because they are: the power of the assembled group. Durkheim's famously provocative conclusion was that in worshipping the sacred, a society is worshipping itself in symbolic form, and that the totem is a representation of the clan.

Whether or not one accepts the reductive conclusion — many do not, and it is fair to say Durkheim proved a function of ritual rather than the origin of religion — the mechanism he identified has held up well. Modern experimental work on synchrony finds that people who move in time together subsequently cooperate more in economic games, report greater liking and similarity, and show elevated pain thresholds, an effect attributed partly to endorphin release. Studies of collective rituals from fire-walking in Spain to the Hindu Thaipusam ceremony in Mauritius have measured synchronised heart rates between performers and even between performers and watching relatives.

Durkheim also drew a distinction still used constantly: positive rites, which bring people into contact with the sacred through offering, communion and celebration, and negative rites, which maintain separation through prohibition, fasting, abstinence and taboo. Most traditions run both, and often sequence them — a period of negative rite preparing participants for a positive one, as with Lent before Easter or Ramadan before Eid.

His third contribution was the observation that rituals cluster at moments of social gathering and that a calendar of rites reproduces the group at intervals. A community that never assembles ceases to be a community in any operative sense; its members may share beliefs but they have no way of knowing they do, no shared emotional history, and no occasion on which obligations are publicly renewed. On this account the point of a weekly service, a monthly meeting or an annual festival is not the content of any single occasion but the recurrence itself.

sections.heading: Sacrifice: destroying value to make something happen
sections.body:
Sacrifice is the most widespread and most theoretically contested class of ritual. The word means literally to make sacred, sacrum facere, and its defining feature is that something of value is removed from ordinary use — killed, burned, buried, poured out, given away or simply forbidden — in a way that cannot be undone. Grain offerings, libations of wine or milk, first fruits, incense, votive objects deposited in rivers and bogs, animals slaughtered on altars, and in some documented cases human beings, all belong to the category.

The classic analysis by Henri Hubert and Marcel Mauss in 1899 identified a common structure. There is a sacrifier, the person on whose behalf the rite is done; a sacrificer, the specialist who performs it; a victim or offering; and a procedure that moves the offering from the profane world into the sacred one, with entry and exit rites protecting the participants at both ends. The victim functions as an intermediary: because it is destroyed it can pass into the sacred realm, and because it stands for the offerer, the offerer participates in that passage without being destroyed.

Several complementary explanations exist, and they are not mutually exclusive. The gift theory, associated with Edward Tylor's phrase do ut des — I give so that you may give — reads sacrifice as exchange with a deity, establishing obligation. The communion theory, from William Robertson Smith, emphasises that most animal sacrifice ends in a shared meal, so the rite is fundamentally about eating together with the god and with each other; in ancient Greece the god received the bones and fat and the community ate the meat, an arrangement the myth of Prometheus at Mecone exists to explain. René Girard's scapegoat theory reads sacrifice as the channelling of internal group violence onto a substitute victim, thereby preventing cycles of reciprocal vengeance. Costly signalling reads it as a public demonstration of commitment.

The last of these makes a testable point: the cost is the mechanism, not an unfortunate side effect. This explains features that other theories struggle with — that offerings must usually be unblemished and valuable rather than surplus, that the offerer should feel the loss, and that a sacrifice made with something worthless is understood everywhere as an insult rather than a bargain.

Sacrifice also survives vigorously in secular form, which is a useful check on any theory that treats it as primitive. Fasting for a cause, giving up income, foregoing career opportunity for a family, running an exhausting charity event, or a leader publicly declining a salary all follow the same logic: the point is the demonstrable, irreversible surrender of something valued. The logic is old, but it is not obsolete, and it operates wherever commitment needs to be made visible.

sections.heading: Purity, pollution and the logic of boundaries
sections.body:
Almost every tradition has rules about cleanness, and to an outsider the rules usually look arbitrary. Why should pork be forbidden but beef permitted, or shellfish unclean while locusts are edible? Why does contact with a corpse, a menstruating woman, a new mother or certain occupations require a period of separation and a washing rite? The most influential answer came from the British anthropologist Mary Douglas in Purity and Danger, published in 1966.

Douglas's argument begins with a definition: dirt is matter out of place. Shoes are not dirty in themselves; shoes on the dining table are. Soil is not dirt in the garden; it is dirt on the carpet. Dirt, therefore, is a by-product of classification. Wherever a society has a system of categories, it generates anomalies that fit nowhere, and anomalies provoke unease. Purity rules are the management of anomaly.

Applying this to the dietary rules of Leviticus, she argued that the clean animals are those that conform fully to their class as defined by the text — land animals with cloven hooves that chew the cud, water creatures with fins and scales, and so on — while the forbidden are those that straddle categories or lack the defining features. The pig has cloven hooves but does not chew the cud; shellfish live in water without fins or scales; creatures that swarm move in ways that belong to no proper domain. On this reading the rules are not hygienic advice misremembered, and not arbitrary tests of obedience, but an expression of an ordered cosmology in which holiness means wholeness and completeness.

Douglas's second major claim is that beliefs about bodily pollution mirror concerns about the social body. Societies anxious about their boundaries — small minorities, groups under threat, communities policing membership — attend closely to what enters and leaves the physical body, regulating food, sex, spitting, blood and excretion. The body is a convenient symbol of any bounded system, and its openings are where the boundary is most at risk.

Not all of Douglas's specific readings have survived scrutiny, and she revised some herself; scholars of the Hebrew Bible have proposed competing accounts stressing the avoidance of death, of blood, or of association with neighbouring cults. The general framework, though, remains the standard tool, and it explains far more than diet: caste rules about contact and commensality, the elaborate purity codes of Shinto and Zoroastrianism, ritual washing before Islamic and Jewish prayer, the requirement to remove shoes before entering a temple or home, and the survival of pollution language in wholly secular contexts, where contamination, cleansing and being tainted are used to describe moral and political matters with no physical dirt involved at all.

sections.heading: How words do things: performative speech and ritual efficacy
sections.body:
Ask what actually makes a marriage, and the answer is disconcerting. No physical change occurs. Yet something real happens, with immediate and enforceable consequences for property, inheritance, taxation, immigration and kinship. The mechanism was analysed by the Oxford philosopher J. L. Austin in lectures published in 1962 as How to Do Things with Words, and it is the sharpest available account of how rituals accomplish anything.

Austin observed that not all sentences describe the world. Some perform actions. "I promise", "I name this ship", "I bet you five pounds", "I pronounce you married", "I hereby resign", "I sentence you to three years" do not report a state of affairs; they bring one about. He called these performative utterances, and noticed they cannot be true or false in the ordinary way. Instead they can be felicitous or infelicitous — they either come off or they do not.

The conditions for felicity are precisely the conditions of ritual. There must be an accepted conventional procedure with a conventional effect. The persons and circumstances must be appropriate to the procedure invoked. The procedure must be executed correctly and completely by all participants. And where the convention requires certain thoughts or intentions, the participants must have them and must subsequently conduct themselves accordingly. A ship-naming performed by a passerby with a bottle of lemonade fails not because the words are false but because the person lacks standing. A marriage performed with the wrong words, by an unauthorised officiant, or with a party who is already married, fails on procedural grounds regardless of anyone's sincerity.

Austin's framework immediately explains why traditions obsess over apparently trivial details: whether the officiant was validly ordained, whether the immersion covered the whole body, whether the correct name was used, whether witnesses were present in the required number. If the effect depends on the procedure being the accepted one correctly executed, then a defect in procedure is a defect in effect, and there is no separate reality to fall back on.

The anthropologist Stanley Tambiah extended this to ritual generally, arguing that rituals are performative in three senses at once: they say something that does something, they stage it dramatically so that participants experience it, and they use indexical symbols whose meaning depends on the context of use, so the same rite attaches to this couple, this child, this dead person. Roy Rappaport pressed further, arguing that because performatives require public convention, ritual is where social facts of any kind — obligation, ownership, office, membership — are manufactured. On this view ritual is not an ornament on top of social structure. It is the mechanism by which social structure exists at all, since a fact that depends on collective acceptance needs a public procedure to create and to change it.

sections.heading: Magic, science and the long argument about what participants think
sections.body:
A recurring dispute in the study of ritual concerns what practitioners actually believe they are doing, and the history of the argument is worth knowing because bad versions of it are still common.

The Victorian intellectualist position, argued by Edward Tylor and elaborated by James Frazer in The Golden Bough from 1890, treated magical ritual as failed science: primitive people, reasoning from mistaken premises, believed that like produces like — sympathetic or imitative magic, as in sticking pins into an effigy — or that things once in contact remain connected — contagious magic, as in working on someone's hair or nail clippings. Frazer proposed an evolutionary sequence from magic through religion to science. The scheme was enormously influential and is now rejected in that form, because it assumes the practitioners are simply making a mistake in physics that they somehow fail to notice across generations of contrary evidence.

Malinowski's Trobriand fieldwork produced the decisive correction. He showed that islanders had a perfectly good practical technology for gardening and canoe-building and used it competently, applying magic in addition, at exactly the points where skill ran out and chance took over. They did not confuse the two. Magic addressed the residue of uncontrollable risk, and its psychological function was to permit confident action in the face of anxiety.

E. E. Evans-Pritchard's study of Zande witchcraft beliefs, published in 1937, made the further point that a ritual system can be internally rational. The Azande did not deny natural causes: they knew a granary collapsed because termites ate its supports. Witchcraft explained the coincidence — why it collapsed at the moment those particular people were sitting beneath it. Their oracles were consulted through elaborate procedures with built-in cross-checks, and apparent failures were absorbed by a battery of secondary elaborations, much as anomalies are absorbed in any explanatory system. Evans-Pritchard's conclusion, that beliefs are rational within a web of assumptions and cannot be judged by pulling one thread out, reshaped the discipline.

The modern position, associated with Dan Sperber, Pascal Boyer and others, is subtler still. Many ritual participants do not hold clear, articulated theories about mechanism at all. Asked why a rite works, people across cultures very often answer that it is what one does, that the ancestors did it, or that it is simply correct — and are unbothered by the absence of a causal story. Ritual knowledge is frequently procedural rather than propositional, held as competence rather than doctrine, in the way that a skilled craftsman's knowledge lives in the hands rather than in a stated theory. Treating every rite as the expression of an underlying belief system is therefore a distortion imported by observers from traditions that happen to be unusually doctrinal.

The practical lesson for understanding an unfamiliar ritual is to resist the modern observer's first question, which is what do they think this achieves. More informative questions are who must be present, what would count as doing it wrongly, and who has authority to say. Those get at the rite's actual social operation.

sections.heading: The cognitive science of ritual: why these actions and not others
sections.body:
Since the 1990s a research programme has tried to explain ritual's specific features in terms of ordinary cognitive machinery, and it has produced some genuinely predictive results alongside claims that remain contested.

One strand concerns the peculiar structure of ritual action itself. Rituals are typically composed of actions whose causal logic is opaque — sprinkling, circling, waving, washing what is not dirty — and performed with a rigidity that resembles nothing so much as the behaviour of people with obsessive-compulsive disorder or the play of young children. Pascal Boyer and Pierre Liénard proposed that ritual engages a hazard-precaution system, an evolved mechanism dedicated to contamination, predation, intrusion and social exclusion, which generates a sense that something must be done and made right. On this account ritualised action captures attention by swamping working memory with low-level detail, which both produces the characteristic absorbed state and blocks the ordinary tendency to ask what the action is for.

A second strand, from Robert McCauley and Thomas Lawson, analyses rituals by where the supernatural agent enters the action structure. Where the agent acts through the officiant on the patient — baptism, ordination, marriage — the rite is a special agent ritual: it is done once, it is irreversible, and it produces high emotional arousal and elaborate staging. Where the participant acts on the agent — offerings, prayers, sacrifices — it is a special patient ritual: repeatable, reversible, lower-key, done frequently. This framework makes concrete predictions about which rites will be repeated and which will not, and the predictions largely hold across the ethnographic record.

A third strand is Harvey Whitehouse's theory of divergent modes of religiosity. He distinguishes the doctrinal mode — frequent, low-arousal, highly repetitive rites, transmitted through language, tending toward orthodoxy, large anonymous communities and a professional clergy — from the imagistic mode — rare, high-arousal, often traumatic rites such as extreme initiations, which are remembered as vivid episodic memories, generate intense bonding within small groups, and resist doctrinal standardisation. Whitehouse's associated concept of identity fusion, a visceral sense of oneness with a group produced by shared dysphoric experience, has been measured in contexts from football fans to Libyan revolutionary battalions, where fused individuals report willingness to fight and die for the group at strikingly high rates.

These accounts should be held with appropriate caution. Sample sizes in the fieldwork are often small, laboratory analogues of ritual are pale imitations, and the replication problems that have affected social psychology touch some of this literature. What is well supported is narrower and still substantial: synchronous movement increases cooperation, painful shared ordeals increase group bonding, and rituals reduce anxiety measurably in people facing uncontrollable outcomes. The last effect has been demonstrated with invented rituals in laboratory settings, which suggests the mechanism does not require any prior belief in the rite's power.

sections.heading: Bodies, rhythm and the making of ritual states
sections.body:
Ritual is done with the body, and the body is not a passive vehicle. A great deal of what rituals accomplish operates below the level of doctrine, through posture, rhythm, breath, fasting, sensory manipulation and repetition, and understanding these mechanisms explains why reading about a rite is nothing like performing one.

Rhythmic entrainment is the best-documented. Drumming, chanting, clapping, marching and dance impose a common tempo on a group, and human beings entrain to external rhythms with unusual facility compared with most animals. Moving in synchrony has measurable consequences: experiments have found increased cooperation in subsequent economic games, greater reported affinity, improved memory for the faces of co-participants, and raised pain thresholds, the last of which is taken as indirect evidence of endorphin release. Anthropologists from William McNeill, who wrote about the effects of close-order drill in armies, to Bronisław Malinowski have noted that the effect does not depend on the participants believing anything in particular.

Second is deliberate physiological manipulation. Fasting alters blood glucose and mood; sustained rhythmic breathing changes carbon dioxide levels and can produce tingling, lightheadedness and altered perception; sleep deprivation degrades ordinary critical filtering; sustained dancing produces exhaustion and endorphin release; extreme temperature in sweat lodges and cold immersion produce strong autonomic responses; pain from scarification, piercing or flagellation produces both endogenous opioid release and, characteristically, an unusually vivid and permanent memory. Psychoactive plants are used in some traditions with great precision — peyote among the Native American Church, ayahuasca in Amazonian and syncretic Brazilian practice, kava in the Pacific — always within an elaborate ritual frame that governs dose, setting and interpretation, which is exactly what modern clinical research on psychedelics has rediscovered under the name of set and setting.

Third is sensory framing. Incense, bells, particular acoustics, darkness punctuated by fire or candlelight, masks, costume and repetitive visual pattern all reduce ordinary environmental cues and increase absorption. Studies in archaeoacoustics suggest that some prehistoric chambered tombs and painted caves have resonant frequencies in the range of a male voice or a drum, and while it is impossible to prove intent, the correlation is striking.

Fourth is habituation and embodied memory. Pierre Bourdieu's concept of habitus captures the result: through repeated bodily practice, dispositions become second nature and are experienced not as rules learned but as the obvious way to be. Someone raised kneeling, bowing, fasting or crossing themselves carries the tradition in their body, and that embodied knowledge persists long after doctrinal assent has lapsed, which is why lapsed adherents so often report that the physical practices are the last thing to go.

Two cautions belong here. These techniques are genuinely powerful, which makes them genuinely dangerous without the safeguards a mature tradition builds around them; prolonged fasting, extreme heat, forced hyperventilation and sleep deprivation have injured and occasionally killed people in unsupervised or commercialised settings. And the effects are not evidence for any particular doctrine, since the same mechanisms produce equally intense experiences in mutually incompatible traditions.

sections.heading: The ritual year: calendars, cycles and the shaping of time
sections.body:
Left alone, time is undifferentiated. Ritual calendars carve it into a shape, and the shape they impose is one of the most consequential things a tradition does, because it determines when a community assembles, when it fasts, when it feasts, when work stops and when the year is understood to begin again.

Most calendars are anchored to astronomical events that any society can observe without instruments. The solstices, when the sun reaches its extremes and appears to stand still for several days around 21 December and 21 June, and the equinoxes near 20 March and 22 September, are marked in an enormous range of traditions. Neolithic monuments including Newgrange in Ireland, where the passage is illuminated at the winter solstice sunrise, and Stonehenge, aligned to the solstice axis, demonstrate that the observations and their ritual marking are at least five thousand years old. Lunar cycles of about 29.5 days give months and drive the Islamic calendar, the Jewish festival cycle and the date of Easter; agricultural events give planting, first fruits and harvest festivals.

The tension between lunar and solar reckoning generates a technical problem every calendrical tradition must solve. Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, eleven short of the solar year, so a purely lunar calendar drifts backwards through the seasons — which is why Ramadan migrates around the year — while a lunisolar calendar must insert an intercalary month periodically, as the Hebrew calendar does seven times in nineteen years. Getting this right was for centuries a matter of religious authority, and calendar reform has repeatedly been a political act: the Julian to Gregorian switch of 1582 was resisted in Protestant states for over a century, and Britain adopted it only in 1752.

Beyond the astronomy, ritual years share a structural rhythm: periods of restriction alternating with periods of release. Lent and Carnival, Ramadan and Eid, Yom Kippur and Sukkot, the agricultural lean season and the harvest feast. The pattern is so consistent that it looks like a design principle rather than a coincidence, and it functions both to store and redistribute resources and to give the year an emotional contour.

Calendars also encode memory. Passover retells an exodus, Independence days retell a founding, remembrance days retell a war, saints' days retell lives. Because these recur annually and involve doing something rather than merely reading something, the past is rehearsed by each generation as a participant rather than received as information. A community's calendar is therefore a reliable map of what it considers itself to be, and changes to it — abolishing a holiday, adding one, moving one — are almost always contested well out of proportion to the practical inconvenience involved.

sections.heading: Domestic, personal and secular ritual
sections.body:
The great public rites are the most studied, but most ritual is small, domestic and unremarkable, and it does a large share of the work. Household rites include the family meal at a fixed hour, the lighting of candles at the start of Sabbath, the shrine in the corner with offerings of rice or incense or flowers, the blessing before eating, the bedtime story in fixed sequence, the shoes left at the door. These are transmitted almost entirely by imitation rather than instruction, and they define what a household feels like from the inside more reliably than any stated belief.

Personal ritual is the same technology applied by one individual. Athletes are famous for it: the same warm-up in the same order, the same equipment placed the same way, the lucky garment. Musicians, surgeons, pilots and soldiers all develop pre-performance sequences. The psychological literature is reasonably clear that these reduce anxiety and improve performance under pressure, and that the effect does not depend on believing in the ritual's causal power — several experiments found benefits from arbitrary sequences invented on the spot by the researchers, provided the participant performed them as a ritual. Checklists in aviation and surgery are a formalised, evidence-based version of the same insight, and the surgical safety checklist introduced through the World Health Organization in 2008 was associated in its initial multi-hospital study with substantial reductions in complications and death.

Secular public ritual is abundant in societies that consider themselves post-religious. Court procedure, with its robes, forms of address, standing when the judge enters and prescribed formulae, is ritual in every technical sense, and its formality serves the same functions: marking the proceedings as extraordinary, constraining what may be said, and generating the legitimacy that makes the verdict binding. Graduations, military parades, oaths of citizenship and office, state funerals, sporting anthems and remembrance silences all follow the classic structure with recognisable separation, liminal and incorporation phases.

Deliberately invented rituals are common and can work, though they face a specific difficulty. The functions ritual performs depend heavily on the sense that the form is given rather than chosen — that one is joining something rather than devising it. A newly minted rite performed once by people who watched it being designed carries little of that weight. What usually solves the problem is repetition and time: an invented rite that is performed unchanged for a decade begins to feel like an inheritance, which is exactly how most traditions began. Humanist funerals, naming ceremonies and secular coming-of-age rites have followed this path with reasonable success, and the successful ones tend to be those that borrowed heavily from existing forms rather than starting from nothing.

sections.heading: How rituals change, and the invention of tradition
sections.body:
Rituals present themselves as unchanging and are in fact constantly changing, and the gap between the two is one of the most interesting things about them. The claim of antiquity is part of the ritual's authority, so participants and specialists alike tend to describe innovations as restorations, and to be sincerely unaware of how recent much of what they do actually is.

The historians Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger gave this the name invention of tradition in a 1983 collection that has shaped the field since. Their examples are startling. Much of the elaborate ceremonial of the British monarchy, universally perceived as immemorial, was designed or substantially reworked between roughly 1870 and 1914, in a period when the monarchy's political power was declining and its symbolic role expanding. Scottish clan tartans as a system of family-specific patterns are largely a nineteenth-century commercial and romantic construction, consolidated around George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh. Many national anthems, flags, remembrance rites and state ceremonies date from the age of nationalism rather than from the deep past they invoke.

The general mechanism has three parts. New situations create needs that existing rites do not meet — a new nation, a new institution, a new technology, a new kind of death. Existing ritual vocabulary is borrowed and recombined, because a wholly novel form would not read as ritual at all. And the result is then attributed to the past, which supplies the authority that a recent invention lacks.

Change also occurs continuously within traditions that believe they are preserving. Liturgical language drifts, then is either updated or deliberately frozen, and either choice has consequences: the Second Vatican Council's authorisation of vernacular liturgy from 1963 transformed Catholic worship and produced a persistent traditionalist reaction. Technology drives change — recorded music, amplification, broadcast services, and most recently the mass improvisation of remote and outdoor rites during the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced traditions to decide urgently which elements were essential and which were incidental. Migration produces change through contact, borrowing and the pressure of a new legal environment.

Two useful distinctions help in analysing any specific change. Traditions weighted towards orthodoxy tolerate wide variation in practice provided doctrine is affirmed, so they change ritual relatively easily and split over creeds. Traditions weighted towards orthopraxy tolerate wide variation in belief provided practice is correct, so they change ritual with great difficulty and split over practice. And there is a difference between change that is negotiated by recognised authority, which tends to be absorbed, and change imposed from outside or introduced without standing, which tends to produce schism. Ritual is durable, but it is not static, and it never has been.

sections.heading: When ritual fails, misfires or harms
sections.body:
Ritual is a powerful social technology and, like any powerful technology, it has characteristic failure modes. Naming them is not hostility to religion; every serious tradition has its own internal literature warning against exactly these.

The first is the misfire in Austin's sense: the procedure was defective, so nothing was accomplished. The officiant lacked authority, a required party was absent or ineligible, the words were wrong, the necessary consent was not given. Traditions handle this with rules for repetition, conditional performance and retroactive validation, and the practical response is almost always the same — establish exactly what was defective, consult whoever has authority to rule on it, and if in doubt repeat the rite properly rather than argue about whether the defect mattered.

The second is hollowing, in which the form is maintained while its meaning drains away and it becomes a chore or a display. Prophetic literature in the Hebrew Bible is largely a sustained complaint about this, insisting that sacrifice without justice is worthless; the Confucian tradition worries about li performed without ren; Christian and Islamic writers make parallel arguments. Hollowing is difficult to detect from outside, because a hollow rite looks exactly like a live one.

The third is scrupulosity, where the anxiety-management function inverts and becomes an anxiety generator. A person becomes trapped in checking, repeating and fearing that a rite was performed incorrectly, in a pattern clinically indistinguishable from obsessive-compulsive disorder and often overlapping with it. This is a recognised clinical presentation, and traditions with pastoral experience typically respond by removing the individual's obligation to judge their own performance and assigning that judgement to a director or confessor. It responds to standard treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder, and someone caught in it should be encouraged toward clinical help rather than more scrupulous practice.

The fourth is genuine harm. Rites involving severe physical ordeal, prolonged fasting, extreme temperature, restraint or psychoactive substances have killed people, particularly when conducted by unqualified operators outside any tradition's own safeguards. Some rites cause lasting injury by design, and female genital cutting is the most consequential contemporary example, defended in some communities on ritual grounds and opposed by essentially the entire medical and human rights consensus. Rituals of exclusion, shunning and shaming can inflict severe damage. And the same machinery that builds solidarity can be turned to mobilising violence, which is why political movements of every character invest so heavily in ceremonial.

The general test is neither antiquity nor sincerity but consequence. A useful set of questions is whether participation is genuinely voluntary and informed, whether anyone is physically harmed, whether the costs fall disproportionately on those with least power, and whether leaving is permitted without destroying the person's entire social world. A rite that fails those questions is not defensible because it is traditional.

guides.title: The Psychology of Religion
guides.summary: An evidence-based survey of how psychology studies religion: the cognitive mechanisms that make god concepts easy to acquire, what ritual and religious experience do to a mind, attachment and development, the contested links to cooperation, meaning and health, and how to read a literature with serious replication problems.

sections.heading: What the field studies, and what it cannot settle
sections.body:
The psychology of religion is the empirical study of religious belief, experience, practice and belonging as psychological phenomena. It asks what happens in a mind that holds a god concept, why such concepts arise so readily in every documented human society, what rituals do to the people who perform them, how religious commitment interacts with health, morality, group loyalty and grief, and how all of this develops across a life. It is a branch of psychology, not of theology, and its methods are the ordinary ones: surveys, experiments, longitudinal cohorts, cross-cultural comparison, ethnography and, more recently, neuroimaging and computational modelling.

The single most important thing to establish at the outset is what this discipline is not doing, because the misunderstanding is pervasive and poisons interpretation in both directions. Explaining the psychological mechanisms that make religious belief easy to acquire says nothing whatever about whether any religious claim is true. This is an instance of the genetic fallacy: the origin of a belief and its truth are separate questions. Human beings have well-documented cognitive machinery that makes them good at arithmetic and at detecting faces, and pointing to that machinery neither vindicates nor undermines the proposition that two plus two is four or that there is a face in front of you. The same holds here. A finding that people readily infer invisible agents does not show gods are illusory, and a finding that religious practice improves wellbeing does not show any doctrine is correct.

Some researchers in the field are believers, some are not, and the better work is written so that its findings are usable by either. Where authors have drawn metaphysical conclusions, as Freud emphatically did and as some contemporary popularisers do, that is an addition to the science rather than a product of it, and this guide will flag such moments.

A second preliminary is definitional. Religion has resisted definition for two centuries. Substantive definitions specify content, typically belief in superhuman agents, and exclude non-theistic traditions such as some forms of Buddhism and Jainism. Functional definitions specify what religion does, typically supplying ultimate meaning and binding communities, and become so broad they swallow nationalism and football. Most working researchers now proceed with a family-resemblance approach, treating religion as a cluster of features, belief in supernatural agents, ritual, moral norms, sacred texts or narratives, communal identity, specialists and sacred spaces, no one of which is strictly necessary.

This matters practically because measurement follows definition. Studies that measure religiosity by weekly attendance at services are measuring something quite different from studies that measure it by self-reported importance of faith or by frequency of private prayer, and these dissociate. A great deal of apparent contradiction in the literature dissolves once you check which variable was actually recorded.

sections.heading: The founding generation: Starbuck, James, Freud and Jung
sections.body:
The field has a clear beginning. In 1899 Edwin Diller Starbuck, a student of William James and of G. Stanley Hall, published The Psychology of Religion, the first book to apply systematic questionnaire methods to religious life. Starbuck collected hundreds of accounts of conversion and found something that surprised his contemporaries: conversion clustered strongly in adolescence, with a modal age around sixteen, which suggested it was bound up with the ordinary developmental turbulence of adolescence rather than being purely a matter of doctrine or divine timing.

William James delivered the Gifford Lectures in Edinburgh in 1901 and 1902 and published them as The Varieties of Religious Experience, still the most widely read book in the field and still worth reading. James made three enduring moves. He insisted on studying religion at the level of individual experience rather than institutions, on the grounds that institutions are secondary crystallisations of what individuals originally felt. He distinguished the healthy-minded temperament, once-born, optimistic, finding the divine in the goodness of things, from the sick soul, twice-born, acutely aware of evil and suffering, requiring a crisis and a rebirth. And he characterised mystical experience by four marks: ineffability, the inability to convey it in words; a noetic quality, the sense of having received knowledge rather than merely feeling something; transiency, since such states rarely last beyond half an hour; and passivity, the sense of being acted upon. James was a pragmatist and judged religious experience by its fruits in conduct, deliberately refusing to rule on its ultimate source.

Sigmund Freud took the opposite line and made the metaphysical claim explicitly. In Totem and Taboo of 1913 he proposed a speculative prehistoric origin story for religion in the killing of a primal father. In The Future of an Illusion of 1927 he argued that religion is wish-fulfilment, a projection of the protective father onto the cosmos in response to helplessness before nature and death, and he described religious ritual as a form of collective obsessional neurosis. Freud's specific historical claims are not taken seriously today and his mechanism is not testable in the form he gave it, but two of his intuitions have survived in modified form: that religious representations recruit emotional systems built for human relationships, and that religion addresses existential helplessness.

Carl Jung broke with Freud partly over this. He treated religious symbols as expressions of archetypes in a collective unconscious and regarded religious life as integral to psychological wholeness, a process he called individuation. Jung's framework is not empirically testable in its central claims and has limited standing in current research, but his sympathetic stance kept a strand of clinical psychology open to religious meaning that Freud's approach had closed.

sections.heading: The cognitive science of religion: agency detection
sections.body:
The most productive research programme of the last thirty years starts from a deceptively simple question: why do supernatural agent concepts appear in every human population ever documented, and why are they so much alike in structure despite wildly differing content? The cognitive science of religion answers that religion is not a specialised adaptation but a by-product of ordinary cognitive systems that evolved for other purposes and happen to make god concepts extremely easy to acquire and transmit.

The first such system is agency detection. Human perception is strongly biased toward interpreting ambiguous patterns and events as caused by an agent, something with beliefs and intentions, rather than by inanimate process. Stewart Guthrie argued in Faces in the Clouds in 1993 that anthropomorphism is a systematic perceptual strategy, and Justin Barrett later named the mechanism the hypersensitive agency detection device. Classic demonstrations include the 1944 Heider and Simmel animation, in which almost every viewer describes two triangles and a circle moving on a screen as characters with motives, chasing and bullying and escaping, despite knowing they are shapes.

The evolutionary logic offered for the bias is asymmetric error cost. If a rustle in the grass is the wind and you infer a predator, you waste a little energy. If it is a predator and you infer wind, you may die. Under that asymmetry, selection favours a detector tuned to fire readily, producing many false positives. Applied to religion, the claim is that a mind primed to see agency behind ambiguous events will readily populate the world with unseen agents: the illness that struck without cause, the storm that spared one village, the sound in an empty house.

This account is intuitive and widely repeated, and it deserves a caution that popular treatments omit. The specific claim that hypersensitive agency detection is the origin of god belief has been challenged. Experiments trying to show that primed agency detection increases supernatural belief have produced mixed results, and critics point out that the bias produces fleeting startle-level inferences, not stable, culturally transmitted, morally concerned deities. The bias plausibly supplies raw material; it does not by itself explain the persistence, elaboration or social role of religious concepts. Most researchers now treat it as one contributing mechanism among several rather than the master explanation, and some regard the evidence as too weak to carry the weight placed on it.

What is much better established is the related capacity of theory of mind, or mentalising: the human ability to represent other minds, their beliefs, desires and intentions, which develops reliably in early childhood. A god is, cognitively speaking, a mind. Once a system for tracking invisible mental states exists, representing a mind without a body demands no new machinery, which is a large part of why such concepts feel natural rather than absurd.

sections.heading: Minimally counterintuitive concepts and why gods are memorable
sections.body:
If religious concepts were merely the output of a jumpy agency detector, they would be as varied and forgettable as dreams. They are not. Across unrelated cultures, supernatural agents share a striking structural profile, and Pascal Boyer's account of why, developed through the 1990s and set out in Religion Explained in 2001, is among the field's most robust contributions.

Boyer's claim is that successful religious concepts are minimally counterintuitive. A mind carries intuitive expectations, sometimes called intuitive ontologies, about broad categories of thing: persons have minds, bodies, and locations and cannot be in two places at once; artefacts do not eat or think; animals grow and die. A concept that violates none of these is boring and unmemorable, like a talking man. A concept that violates too many is incoherent and hard to hold, like an invisible weeping mountain that exists only on Tuesdays, remembers the future and is made of grief. The sweet spot is a concept that keeps almost all default expectations intact and breaks one or two. A statue that hears prayers is a perfectly ordinary artefact plus one mental property. A ghost is an ordinary person minus a body. A god is an ordinary mind with unlimited knowledge or reach.

The crucial point is that the intact expectations do the heavy lifting. Because the concept is mostly a person, the whole apparatus of social reasoning applies automatically: you can infer what it wants, fear its anger, seek its favour, feel watched by it. That rich inferential payload comes free, which is why these concepts are cognitively cheap and behaviourally powerful.

The theory generates a testable prediction about memory and transmission, and it has been tested. Barrett and Nyhof in 2001, and a series of studies after, presented participants with stories containing intuitive, minimally counterintuitive and maximally counterintuitive items, then tested recall immediately and after delays of days or months. Minimally counterintuitive items were typically recalled best, and their advantage grew over time and across retellings, which is the pattern needed for cultural transmission. Later work complicated the picture: the effect is sensitive to context, to how many counterintuitive items a narrative contains, and to whether the material is presented as a list or a story, and some studies find intuitive items recalled equally well. The consensus is that a real but moderate memory advantage exists, concentrated in narratives with a small proportion of counterintuitive elements, which is exactly the proportion found in actual folktales and scriptures.

The theory explains a genuine puzzle: why the world's supernatural beings are so unimaginative. Gods, spirits and ancestors are overwhelmingly person-like, with a handful of superpowers, rather than the truly alien entities an unconstrained imagination might produce. Cultural selection has filtered for what minds can hold and retell.

sections.heading: Intuition, reflection and the contested analytic-thinking effect
sections.body:
Alongside content-based explanations sits a process-based one. Dual-process theories of cognition, popularised by Daniel Kahneman as System 1 and System 2, distinguish fast, automatic, intuitive processing from slow, effortful, reflective processing. Applied to religion, the proposal has been that supernatural belief is intuitively natural and that reflective thinking tends to override it, so individual differences in the disposition to reflect should predict disbelief.

The most-cited evidence uses the Cognitive Reflection Test, a three-item task devised by Shane Frederick in 2005 in which each question has an intuitively compelling wrong answer. The bat-and-ball item is the famous one: a bat and a ball cost one dollar ten in total, the bat costs one dollar more than the ball, so how much does the ball cost. The intuitive answer of ten cents is wrong, since that would make the bat one dollar ten and the total one dollar twenty; the correct answer is five cents. Shenhav, Rand and Greene reported in 2012 that lower scores on this test predicted stronger belief in God. Gervais and Norenzayan published in Science the same year a set of experiments claiming that experimentally inducing analytic thinking, for example by having people view Rodin's Thinker or read text in a hard-to-read font, reduced reported religious belief.

This is one of the places where honesty about the state of the evidence matters most, because the finding entered popular writing as settled and is not. The experimental priming results have fared badly. A large preregistered replication by Sanchez and colleagues in 2017, and other independent attempts, failed to reproduce the effect of the disfluent font and the Thinker image on belief. The broader replication crisis in social psychology hit this literature hard, and manipulations that were reported as robust in samples of a few dozen have generally not survived preregistered tests with thousands of participants.

What has held up better is the correlational finding. Across many large samples in multiple countries, people who score higher on reflective-thinking measures report somewhat weaker religious belief, with correlations typically modest, in the range of minus 0.1 to minus 0.2. That is a real association but a small one, meaning reflective disposition accounts for a few percent of the variance in belief and leaves the great majority unexplained. It is also correlational, so the causal direction is not established: reflective people may become less religious, or people raised in less religious environments may cultivate reflection, or education and social context may drive both.

Cross-cultural work has further complicated matters, finding the association weak or absent in some non-Western samples, which suggests it may reflect a particular cultural relationship between religiosity and education rather than a universal feature of cognition.

sections.heading: Ritual: what repetition and arousal do to a mind
sections.body:
Ritual is arguably more central to religion than belief, and it is certainly more tractable to study. A ritual is a formalised, repeated, rule-governed sequence of actions whose form is prescribed and whose causal connection to any practical outcome is opaque to participants. That opacity is the defining feature: cooking has steps with visible reasons, whereas ritual steps must be done because they must be done.

Several psychological effects of ritual are well documented. Repetition and prescribed form reduce uncertainty, and there is evidence that people turn to ritualised behaviour more under conditions of anxiety and low control, a finding that echoes Bronisław Malinowski's classic observation among Trobriand fishermen that elaborate magic accompanied dangerous open-sea fishing but not safe lagoon fishing. Experimental work has found that performing a ritual before a stressful task can reduce anxiety and improve performance, though effect sizes are modest and some results are contested.

Synchrony is a second mechanism with good evidence. Moving in time with others, in chanting, singing, dancing, marching or bowing, reliably increases feelings of affiliation, trust and cooperation in laboratory tasks, an effect demonstrated in adults and in infants as young as fourteen months. Collective singing and vigorous coordinated movement also raise pain thresholds, a proxy for endorphin release, and small-group singing produces measurable increases in social bonding.

Harvey Whitehouse's modes of religiosity theory organises much of this. He distinguishes the doctrinal mode, characterised by frequent, low-arousal, repetitive ritual such as weekly worship, which builds semantic memory for doctrine, sustains large anonymous communities and depends on centralised authority and orthodoxy; and the imagistic mode, characterised by rare, high-arousal, often painful or terrifying ritual such as initiation ordeals, which creates vivid episodic flashbulb memories and forges intense bonds within small groups. The rare, dysphoric rituals are associated with what Whitehouse calls identity fusion, a visceral sense of oneness with the group that predicts extreme self-sacrifice, including willingness to fight and die, in survey work among veterans and participants in violent conflict.

A third framework is costly signalling theory, drawn from evolutionary biology. Because private commitment is invisible and cheap talk is easy, groups come to favour displays that are too expensive for a free-rider to fake: fasting, celibacy, dietary restriction, tithing, distinctive dress and grooming, lengthy daily prayer, painful initiation. Richard Sosis's study of nineteenth-century American communes found that religious communes survived considerably longer than secular ones, with about thirty-nine percent of religious communes still functioning after twenty years against six percent of secular ones, and that among religious communes the number of costly requirements imposed predicted longevity, whereas among secular communes it did not. Related work on Israeli kibbutzim found members of religious kibbutzim more cooperative in economic games than members of secular ones. The interpretation is that costly requirements screen out the uncommitted and thereby stabilise cooperation, though these samples are historical or small and the inference remains correlational.

sections.heading: Religious and mystical experience, and the brain
sections.body:
Reported experiences of the sacred range from a quiet sense of presence during prayer to overwhelming episodes of unity, dissolution of self and certainty of contact with something ultimate. Surveys in the United States and Britain have consistently found that a third to a half of adults report at least one experience they describe as religious, spiritual or mystical, so these are common rather than exotic.

The most striking laboratory work uses psychedelics. Walter Pahnke's Good Friday Experiment in 1962, conducted at Boston University's Marsh Chapel under Timothy Leary's supervision, gave psilocybin or an active placebo to twenty theology students during a service; those receiving psilocybin reported experiences scoring far higher on mysticism measures, and a long-term follow-up decades later found most still rated it among the most spiritually significant events of their lives. The study had serious methodological weaknesses, including a broken blind and an adverse reaction that went unreported for years. Rigorous modern replication came from Roland Griffiths and colleagues at Johns Hopkins from 2006 onward, using double-blind designs with methylphenidate as an active comparator. About two-thirds of healthy volunteers given a high dose of psilocybin rated the session among the five most personally and spiritually meaningful experiences of their lives, comparable to the birth of a child, and at fourteen months most reported sustained positive changes in attitude and behaviour corroborated by community observers. The experiences map closely onto James's four marks.

Neuroimaging of religious states has produced less than its publicity suggests. Andrew Newberg's SPECT studies of Franciscan nuns in prayer and Tibetan monks in meditation reported decreased activity in parietal regions associated with spatial self-location, offered as a correlate of the loss of self-boundary. Sample sizes were very small. Studies of self-identified believers engaged in prayer generally show recruitment of ordinary social-cognitive and mentalising networks rather than any dedicated region, which is theoretically interesting precisely because it is unremarkable: praying looks like talking to someone.

Two widely circulated claims deserve correction. The first is the God helmet, Michael Persinger's device applying weak magnetic fields to the temporal lobes and reported to induce a sensed presence. A controlled double-blind study by Granqvist and colleagues in 2005 found that suggestibility, not the magnetic field, predicted the experience, and that participants reported presences with the device switched off. The second is the temporal lobe epilepsy connection. Intense religious experience does occur in some patients around seizures, and the Geschwind syndrome describes a cluster including hyperreligiosity, but the proportion of epilepsy patients affected is small and the retrospective diagnosis of historical religious figures on this basis is speculation rather than evidence.

The honest summary is that religious experience is real, common, produces lasting effects, and has identifiable neural correlates that are the same systems used for selfhood, emotion and social cognition. Nothing in the imaging adjudicates what, if anything, is being experienced.

sections.heading: Attachment: God as a relationship
sections.body:
One of the most fruitful transplants into this field is attachment theory, developed by John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth to describe the bond between infant and caregiver. Bowlby proposed an innate behavioural system: the infant maintains proximity to a caregiver, uses that caregiver as a secure base for exploration and as a safe haven in distress, and protests separation. Ainsworth's Strange Situation procedure identified individual differences, broadly secure, anxious-ambivalent and avoidant patterns, which show meaningful continuity into adult relationships.

Lee Kirkpatrick argued from the early 1990s that a personal God functions psychologically as an attachment figure and satisfies the defining criteria remarkably well. Believers seek proximity through prayer, worship and sacred space; turn to God as a safe haven in illness, bereavement and fear, with prayer sharply increasing in crisis; treat faith as a secure base licensing confidence in exploration and risk; and experience the sense of God's absence, the dark night of the soul, as something very like separation distress. God is moreover conceived as stronger and wiser, the classic attachment-figure profile.

Two competing hypotheses were proposed about how earthly attachment history relates to religious attachment. The correspondence hypothesis predicts continuity: securely attached people develop secure, loving images of God, while insecurely attached people develop anxious or distant ones, because the same internal working models are applied. The compensation hypothesis predicts the opposite for a subset: people with insecure or disrupted attachments turn to God to supply the security a caregiver did not, and should therefore be over-represented among sudden, emotionally intense converts.

The evidence supports both, operating in different circumstances, which is a more interesting result than either alone. Correspondence generally holds for the ordinary, gradual, socialised religiosity of people raised in a faith, and measures of attachment security correlate positively with loving God images and negatively with anxious ones. Compensation shows up specifically in sudden conversion: Kirkpatrick and Granqvist found that adults reporting insecure childhood attachment and, particularly, having had non-religious parents were markedly over-represented among those reporting abrupt conversions in adulthood, often during a period of personal crisis or after the loss of a relationship. Granqvist's later work found that experimentally activating separation distress increased religious seeking among insecurely attached participants but not securely attached ones.

The framework has practical clinical value. It predicts that bereavement, divorce and serious illness will intensify religious behaviour, which they reliably do. It predicts that God images are not merely doctrinal but emotional, so two members of the same congregation reciting identical creeds may experience utterly different relationships, one warm and one punitive. And it makes sense of the phenomenon of religious deconversion following a crisis of trust, which follows the pattern of relationship rupture more closely than that of argument.

sections.heading: Development and conversion: how belief is acquired and changed
sections.body:
Children do not receive religion as adults receive an argument. They acquire it through the same channels as everything else about the social world: testimony from trusted adults, participation in practice, and inference from an already-structured mind.

Several early-emerging cognitive tendencies make religious content easy to absorb. Deborah Kelemen's work documents promiscuous teleology: preschool children strongly prefer purpose-based explanations for natural objects, agreeing that rocks are pointy so animals will not sit on them and that rain exists so plants can grow. This preference is not merely a repetition of adult teaching, appears in children of non-religious parents, and re-emerges in adults under time pressure, suggesting it is a default the educated mind learns to suppress rather than an idea that must be taught. Children also show early essentialism about categories and mind-body dualism, judging that mental properties such as knowing and loving might continue after biological death while bodily properties do not, a pattern Jesse Bering documented in interviews about a dead mouse puppet.

Justin Barrett's much-discussed preparedness hypothesis holds that these tendencies make children receptive to god concepts rather than blank. His early studies suggested children under about five attribute superknowledge to God more readily than adults expect, though the interpretation is disputed, and subsequent cross-cultural work in Israel, Greece and among Yukatek Maya children shows the developmental trajectory varies with the religious content of the local culture. The defensible conclusion is that children are receptive, not that they are natural theists.

Testimony is the dominant channel. Paul Harris's research shows children rationally calibrate trust in testimony, believing in unobservable entities such as germs and oxygen on the same basis as they believe in angels, namely adult consensus and confident assertion. Where adults speak unanimously and without hedging, children believe; where adults hedge, children treat the entity as fictional. This straightforwardly predicts the strongest single demographic finding in the field: the best predictor of an adult's religion is the religion of their parents and community.

Conversion research distinguishes gradual socialisation, which is by far the commonest route, from sudden conversion, the dramatic form that dominates popular imagination and Starbuck's original data. The Lofland and Stark model of 1965, built from fieldwork on a small new religious movement, proposed a sequence in which enduring tensions, a religious problem-solving perspective and a seekership orientation predispose a person, and then a turning point, the formation of affective bonds with members, weakening of outside attachments and intensive interaction complete the process. Its central insight has held: conversion typically follows relationships rather than arguments. Deconversion research, a much younger literature, finds intellectual doubt, moral objection to a community's conduct, and unanswered suffering as recurring themes, and finds the process often protracted and socially costly.

sections.heading: Religion and cooperation: the big gods hypothesis and its critics
sections.body:
Human societies grew from bands of a few dozen kin to cities of millions of strangers in a few thousand years, and this poses a genuine puzzle for theories of cooperation. Reputation and reciprocity police behaviour effectively in small groups where everyone is observed; they work poorly among anonymous strangers. The supernatural monitoring hypothesis, developed by Ara Norenzayan, Azim Shariff and colleagues and set out in Norenzayan's Big Gods of 2013, proposes that belief in powerful, morally concerned, punitive gods who see everything extended the reach of reputational policing by installing a watcher who is never absent.

Several strands of evidence were assembled.
